newsitem.title: BELARUS: Russia thinks about Belarus in arguing with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia thinks about Belarus in arguing with NATO.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Monday that in opposing NATO expansion plans, Moscow was also defending the interests of neighbouring Belarus.

"We are still insisting on our demands in order not to worsen the geopolitical situation," Primakov told a news conference in the Belarussian capital Minsk in a reference to Russia's objections to NATO plans to expand eastwards.
"We are trying to minimise the possible consequences and we are thinking not only about Russia but about Belarus as well, with which we are moving towards a union."
Primakov's trip to Minsk followed the signing last Wednesday of a Union Treaty between Russia and Belarus by Presidents Boris Yeltsin and Alexander Lukashenko.
The original 17-page draft was radically amended in hectic last-minute negotiations and the final accord sounded like a declaration of intent rather than a binding treaty.
Moscow made the 11th hour changes to the document after liberals in the government expressed fears it might make integration too fast and give Lukashenko a say in decisions affecting Russia.

On Friday Yeltsin, clearly embarrassed at having to get himself out of a diplomatic corner, sacked his top foreign policy adviser Dmitry Ryurikov, accused by Kremlin sources of having tried to force the pace of integration.
Yeltsin also blamed unnamed politicians for trying to push Russia towards integration with its backward western neighbour.
Primakov was not directly involved in the preparation of the treaty, concentrating on the dispute with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

The 16-nation western defence alliance is expected to invite at least three of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to begin NATO membership negotiations at a summit in Madrid in July.

Primakov is trying to negotiate conditions for the planned eastward expansion of NATO that would inflict minimal damage and humiliation on Russia. But he reiterated in Minsk that this did not mean Moscow would lift its objections to the plan, which it sees as an aggressive move which could threaten its security.
"Russia-NATO talks are being carried out not in order to extract a payment for removing our demands," he said.
He took a cautious line on Russia's planned union with Belarus, which borders Poland, the Baltic states of Latvia and Estonia, Russia and Ukraine.
"The form of the union depends on the will of the people and will be decided in the future, not today or tomorrow," he said.
Primakov declined to comment on Lukashenko's crackdown on the opposition and some of the media, particularly Russian journalists, saying: "The internal problems of Belarus are its internal problems."
